EXCELLENCE
The design & layout of IndianOil’s Integrated
Annual Report is inspired by its business
theme “Towards Mission Excellence”.
The theme reflects a purposeful journey of
transformation to meet the transition of the
Energy industry, growth and achievement.

At its core, the vibrant multicoloured swish symbolizes the collective
energy, innovation, and commitment of our people. Its dynamic
flow reflects the convergence of varied strengths, perspectives,
and capabilities that power the organisation forward. The colours
and movement reflect growth on various fronts like technology,
customer values and organisational capability. This diverse growth
reflects our commitment to continuously expanding our horizons,
strengthening our foundations, and creating lasting impact across
every dimension of the business. This swish evolves into a defined
pathway, representing a manifold, vibrant strategic direction and the
disciplined execution required to achieve the mission.

At the culmination of this vibrant way forward, the sprinting runner
symbolizes agility, determination, and the relentless pursuit of
excellence. The runner embodies individuals and teams who seize
opportunities, overcome challenges, and accelerate progress with
purpose. Moving forward with confidence, the figure reflects our
collective drive to convert potential into remarkable performance and
aspirations into spectacular achievements.

The upward trajectory of the pathway upholds our commitment to
transitioning sustainably; advancing responsibly while balancing
growth, innovation, and long-term stewardship. It represents our
resolve to build enduring success by creating value that is resilient,
responsible, and future-ready.

Together, the design translates a powerful narrative of momentum,
multidimensional growth, execution excellence, and sustainable
progress. Capturing the essence of Towards Mission Excellence, it
charts a purposeful journey where opportunities are transformed into
results, achievements are sustained, and long-term value is created.

About IndianOil

The Energy Behind India’s Progress
IndianOil holds ‘Maharatna’ status, the highest classification accorded to a
Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE) in India. Over the decades, IndianOil
has evolved into one of the country’s largest and most strategically significant
enterprises, playing a vital role in supporting energy access, industrial activity,
economic development and mobility across the nation.

Our Businesses

A Portfolio Advancing
Mission Excellence
India’s demand for energy spans fuels, gas, petrochemicals and newer forms
of energy. IndianOil operates across these markets. Our refining and marketing
businesses account for the largest share of operations today, while investments
in petrochemicals, natural gas, upstream assets and new energy are widening
the sources of future business.


                                                REFINING, PIPELINES AND MARKETING
                                                Our refineries process a diverse crude slate into fuels, feedstocks and
                                                speciality products for India’s energy markets. Ongoing capacity additions
                                                at Panipat, Gujarat and Barauni are taking our group refining capacity
                                                towards ~98 MMTPA, providing headroom for demand growth and greater
                                                integration with petrochemicals. Our pipeline network connects crude and
                                                product movement with major consumption centres, providing an efficient
                                                mode of bulk transportation.

                                                Marketing completes this integrated chain. Through our retail outlets,
                                                aviation fuelling facilities and an extensive LPG distribution network, we
                                                serve mobility, industrial, aviation and household demand across the
                                                country. Investments across refining, pipelines and market infrastructure
                                                are directed towards maintaining supply reliability while preparing these
                                                businesses for changing product and energy requirements.




                                                PETROCHEMICALS
                                                Petrochemicals increase the value derived from refinery streams and
                                                broaden our participation beyond transportation fuels. Our portfolio spans
                                                polymers, fibre intermediates and performance chemicals, including PP,
                                                PX/PTA, LAB and PBR, serving applications across packaging, textiles,
                                                plastics and industrial manufacturing.

                                                New capacity and deeper refinery-petrochemical integration are widening
                                                the product portfolio and increasing conversion of refinery streams into
                                                higher-value products. Development of speciality chemicals and indigenous
                                                catalysts also addresses selected import dependencies.

 NATURAL GAS
 Our natural gas business spans LNG import and regasification, gas
 marketing and City Gas Distribution. The 5 MMTPA Ennore LNG terminal
 of our JV Company provides import and regasification infrastructure in
 southern India, while our pipeline connectivity and marketing activities
 connect gas supply with industrial and commercial demand.

 The Company alongwith its joint ventures have authorisation across 49
 geographical areas for City Gas Distribution. These businesses extend
 gas access to households, transport and industry and broaden IndianOil’s
 participation across the gas value chain.




 EXPLORATION AND PRODUCTION (E&P)
 Our upstream portfolio consist of direct participation in oil and gas
 resources in India and overseas. Currently, we have interests across 12
 domestic and 10 overseas E&P blocks, providing exposure to different
 resource basins and geographies.

 The portfolio complements our downstream scale by extending our
 upstream presence in the hydrocarbon value chain. Partnerships, technology
 deployment and disciplined development of producing and prospective
 assets remain central to how we manage this portfolio and its contribution
 to long-term energy supply.




 ALTERNATIVE ENERGY AND OTHER BUSINESSES
 Our portfolio is extending into energy forms that are expected to assume
 a larger role in India’s evolving energy mix. Investments span renewable
 power, green hydrogen, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), biofuels,
 compressed biogas and electric mobility, alongside other emerging
 business opportunities.

 Development activities have commenced for 1 GW of renewable energy
 capacity through Wholly owned Subsidiary Terra Clean Ltd., with preparatory
 work underway for an additional 4.3 GW. We are also developing green
 hydrogen at Panipat, advancing biofuel and CBG pathways and participating
 in hydrogen mobility trials. IndianOil became the first company in India to
 obtain ISCC CORSIA certification for SAF production at Panipat Refinery.

 Global Energy Footprint

 Taking Expertise Worldwide
 IndianOil’s international operations encompass fuel marketing, lubricants,
 aviation fuels, LPG, exploration and production, and global energy trade.
 Through its overseas subsidiaries, joint ventures, and participating interests, the
 Company has established a strategic presence in South Asia, the Indian Ocean
 region, and the Middle East, while also maintaining interests in international
 exploration assets. In addition, IndianOil actively undertakes crude oil sourcing
 and petroleum product trading in key global markets.

IndianOil Over the Years

Journey of Growth
IndianOil’s growth has been intrinsically linked with India’s economic growth,
playing a pivotal role in strengthening the nation’s energy security and
advancing its vision of self-reliance. Indian Oil Corporation Limited was
formed on September 1, 1964, upon the merger of Indian Refineries Limited
(incorporated in 1958) with Indian Oil Company Limited (incorporated in
1959), to build India’s refining capabilities and develop a robust petroleum
distribution network.

From early refineries at Guwahati, Barauni, and Koyali, IndianOil has expanded steadily over the decades into a diversified, integrated
energy enterprise with a nationwide presence. In recognition of its scale, strategic importance, and operational excellence, the
Government of India conferred the prestigious ‘Maharatna’ status on IndianOil in 2010, a distinction reserved for the country’s largest
and most globally competitive public sector enterprises. The Company has also consistently featured among the Fortune Global 500,
reflecting its growing global stature.

Today, IndianOil operates one of India’s largest integrated energy businesses, continuing to drive the nation’s progress through reliable
energy solutions while contributing to the vision of an Atmanirbhar (self-reliant) India.

Through every phase of India’s energy transition—from kerosene lighting to clean cooking with LPG, from leaded fuels to BS-VI fuels,
and now towards cleaner and greener solutions—IndianOil’s product portfolio has evolved to reflect the nation’s changing aspirations.
Over the decades, the Company has earned the confidence of generations of Indians, establishing itself as one of the country’s most
trusted energy brand.

Strategic Capital Trade-offs

The Inter-connected Nature of
Value Creation
Our business decisions involve choices between near-term requirements
and long-term value. Capital allocated to one area can affect the availability,
quality or use of other capitals. We consider these interdependencies when
allocating resources across existing operations, capacity additions and
emerging energy businesses.

01     BALANCING CORE GROWTH WITH NEW ENERGY INVESTMENT

       Refining expansion, petrochemical integration and investments in renewables,                             Capital Deployed
       green hydrogen and SAF place competing demands on Financial Capital. Capital
       allocation must balance businesses serving India’s current energy demand with
       investments in emerging energy pathways.
                                                                                                                Capitals Affected

       THE TRADE-OFF
       Near-term capital intensity            Diversification of future energy portfolio




02     ADDING CAPACITY WHILE MANAGING RESOURCE INTENSITY

       Additional refining and petrochemical capacity increases the asset base available                        Capital Deployed
       to serve projected demand. It also raises the importance of energy efficiency,
       asset reliability and responsible resource use across a larger operating footprint.

                                                                                                                Capitals Affected

       THE TRADE-OFF
       Capacity for growing demand                Resource and energy requirements

 STAKEHOLDER
 ENGAGEMENT
IndianOil’s role in India’s energy ecosystem
extends across consumers, industries,
communities, business partners, investors
and public institutions. Decisions relating to
growth, operations, investments and future
energy pathways are shaped by a broad range
of perspectives and expectations emerging
from this ecosystem.
These considerations are evaluated alongside
the resources and relationships that sustain the
business, providing the context for identifying
the matters that warrant the highest degree
of management attention. The resulting
priorities influence how capital is allocated,
how performance is assessed and how value
is created across economic, environmental
and social dimensions.

Empowering Relationships, Enabling Growth

Aligning stakeholder
expectations with business
Material matters sit at the intersection of stakeholder expectations and the
resources employed by the business. Our materiality assessment provides
a structured process for evaluating the economic, environmental, social and
governance matters that are most relevant to IndianOil and its stakeholders.
The assessment considers both the implications of these matters for our
business performance and the impact of our activities on the economy,
environment and society.

MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT

We undertook a double materiality assessment aligned with recognised global frameworks during 2024-25. Inputs from stakeholders,
leadership deliberations and management reviews formed the basis for evaluating and prioritising material matters within our operating
context. For 2025-26, the materiality assessment was revisited to reflect the evolving sustainability landscape and business context
of IndianOil. While the overall set of material topics remains broadly consistent with prior years, certain topics have been redefined to
better capture emerging and evolving risks.

The identified material matters serve as an important reference point for our business planning, resource allocation, risk oversight and
performance evaluation across the organisation.

Customers
India’s energy demand is diverse in both scale and application.
Households require reliable access to cooking fuel, transport
users depend on uninterrupted fuel availability, industries
rely on energy and feedstock supplies, while commercial
establishments, aviation operators and institutional customers
require specialised products and service support. Meeting
these varied requirements calls for a combination of extensive
physical infrastructure, supply reliability, product quality, digital
accessibility and responsive customer service.
Our customer engagement approach is built around three considerations: availability,
reliability and convenience. Investments in distribution infrastructure, digital interfaces,
alternative energy solutions and service delivery mechanisms are directed towards
ensuring that customers can access products and services efficiently while adapting to
evolving energy consumption patterns and mobility requirements.

SERVING A DIVERSE CUSTOMER BASE
Our customer base spans households, mobility users, industrial
consumers, commercial establishments, aviation operators,
government institutions and energy-intensive sectors. Customer
requirements differ significantly across these segments, requiring
differentiated products, distribution models and service channels.

Household customers access LPG, PNG and related services
through an extensive distribution network. Mobility customers utilise
retail fuels, lubricants, CNG, LNG, EV charging and battery-swapping
facilities through an expanding retail infrastructure. Industrial
and commercial customers utilise natural gas, petrochemicals,
bitumen, specialty products and bulk fuel supplies that support
manufacturing, infrastructure and transportation activities. Aviation
and institutional customers depend on uninterrupted product
availability, operational reliability and specialised services tailored
to their requirements.

This diversity necessitates continuous assessment of customer
expectations, consumption trends and service requirements.
Investments in customer infrastructure, digital platforms and
product innovation are therefore guided by changing patterns of
demand across customer segments.

MISSION LiFE (LIFESTYLE FOR
ENVIRONMENT) IN ACTION
Mission LiFE forms an important part of how we bring environmental
responsibility into our operations, workplaces and customer
touchpoints. Through measures covering operational practices,
ecological restoration, community participation and resource
efficiency, we are encouraging behavioural change across our
business and among the communities we serve.

Embedding Responsible Practices Across Operations
We are embedding Mission LiFE across our operations through
measures covering waste management, reduction of single-
use plastics and greater environmental awareness. Our efforts
extend across corporate offices, administrative establishments
and refining units, while our network of more than 30,000 retail
outlets is progressing towards plastic-free operations. Mission
LiFE awareness campaigns across retail outlets and regional
offices, together with Pollution Under Control (PUC) testing drives
organised across our fuel stations, are encouraging cleaner mobility
and greater public participation.

IndianOil’s SPRINT Fuelling India’s Growth

Energising India’s Next                                                                                                      MD&A




Growth Chapter
India remains one of the world’s most compelling long-term growth markets.
Sustained economic expansion, rising incomes, rapid industrialisation,
infrastructure development, and increasing mobility continue to drive demand
across the economy. Unlike many mature markets, where energy consumption
has stabilised, India continues to generate new sources of energy demand,
creating significant long-term opportunities across fuels, feedstocks, energy
infrastructure, and related services.
The scale of this opportunity extends well beyond conventional measures of economic growth. Expanding transportation networks,
manufacturing investments, urban development, aviation growth, logistics modernisation and increasing digitalisation are creating
sustained demand across a broad spectrum of energy products. As India’s economy becomes larger and more diversified, its energy
needs are evolving in both scale and complexity, creating opportunities across the full spectrum of established and emerging
energy businesses.

POSITIONING INDIANOIL IN THIS LANDSCAPE
IndianOil’s portfolio today spans refining, petrochemicals, pipelines, gas, fuel marketing and emerging energy businesses, supported by one
of the largest investment programmes in the Company’s history. Managing this portfolio requires simultaneous oversight of capital projects,
operating assets, commercial activities and new business initiatives, each with distinct operating and financial requirements.

As investment intensity increases, performance depends not only on capital deployment but equally on project delivery, asset utilisation, cost
management and commercial execution across business segments.

PROJECT SPRINT
Project SPRINT was launched in April 2025 as a three-year Company-wide programme aimed at improving profitability, productivity and capital
efficiency through a common set of priorities, goals and accountability mechanisms.

The programme integrates 25 strategic goals across refining, marketing, pipelines and business development, while bringing together Human
Resources, Finance, Information Systems and Research & Development under a common execution framework. Its objective is straightforward:
improve coordination across functions and businesses while accelerating execution across the Company.



SPRINT is organised around six inter-connected priorities that collectively address the key
drivers of long-term business performance.

PROGRESS DURING 2025-26
Project SPRINT entered its first year of implementation with a focus on improving business performance through profitable growth,
sharper execution and cost optimisation. The programme aligned 25 strategic goals across business verticals and enabling functions,
creating a common agenda for execution across the Company.

The emphasis on planning, milestone tracking, performance reviews and accountability introduced greater discipline into how priorities
are executed and monitored. This translated into improvements across commercial performance, operating efficiency, customer
engagement, technology adoption, workforce capability and future growth initiatives.


   STRENGTHENING CORE BUSINESSES

2025-26 brought higher volumes across IndianOil’s refining, pipeline and gas businesses, alongside additions to its distribution network
and market presence across selected product categories. Activities under this pillar remained focused on businesses that continue
to account for the largest share of the Company operations and asset base.

The year also saw movement across businesses expected to assume a larger role in the portfolio over time. Sustainable Aviation Fuel,
Compressed Biogas, renewable energy and natural gas formed part of this effort, while workforce reskilling and Artificial Intelligence
adoption progressed across enabling functions.

    PROPELLING COST OPTIMISATION

Cost discipline under this pillar centred on lowering the operating cost of existing assets while preserving investment capacity across
growth and transition businesses. The effort extended across refining, LPG, aviation and pipeline operations, with energy performance
emerging as a key contributor to both cost reduction and emissions management.

The year’s outcomes pointed to tighter control over energy consumption, operating expenditure and maintenance costs across businesses.
Savings generated through these measures supported investments in petrochemicals, natural gas, green hydrogen, renewables and
bio-energy, in line with the cost leadership philosophy articulated under SPRINT.

  REINFORCING CUSTOMER CENTRICITY

Customer engagement during the year focused on reliability of supply, service responsiveness and deeper interaction across retail
and institutional segments. Digital interventions at retail outlets, non-fuel offerings, and loyalty programmes formed part of the effort
to strengthen customer engagement across retail and fleet businesses.

The disruptions arising from the West Asia crisis provided an early test of these arrangements. Higher LPG production at refineries,
upgrades to IT systems to manage booking volumes and the creation of a dedicated grievance resolution cell helped to ensure
uninterrupted supplies and faster customer response during periods of uncertainty.

  INTEGRATING TECHNOLOGY AND INNOVATION

Technology moved closer to the operating core of the business, with applications extending from refinery units and process optimisation
to procurement, safety and governance systems. The emphasis shifted from technology adoption in isolation to deployment across
assets, operations and decision-making processes.

Research activities increasingly progressed beyond laboratories and into commercial and industrial applications. Process technologies,
catalysts and energy transition solutions advanced through pilot plants, commercial pathways and operating deployments, supported
by internal capabilities, startup engagement, and external partnerships.

R&D is increasingly tied to commercial and business outcomes under the SPRINT framework. Technology commercialisation generated

as Type II fuel for export vehicles, Bajaj for SERVO 4T 10W-30(B) and 20W-50(B), JCMAS for SERVO Hydrex J and Hydrex S, and Tata
Steel for SERVO Steerol C 105 widened market access and opened business opportunities. Our intellectual property portfolio crossed
2,000 IP assets, with 123 patents granted during 2025-26, taking cumulative patent grants to 1,729.




  NURTURING LEADERSHIP AND TALENT

Changes under this pillar became visible in the way work was organised, decisions were made and capabilities were developed across
the organisation. Learning moved closer to day-to-day responsibilities, while emerging businesses and technologies created demand
for new skills across functions and operating units.

Greater ownership at the operating level was accompanied by the wider use of digital learning platforms and role-based capability
development. Cross-functional working gained prominence across renewables, Artificial Intelligence and new business areas, while
leadership practices placed greater emphasis on agility, empowerment and faster decision-making.

  TRANSITION READY

IndianOil’s transition agenda remained closely aligned with India’s energy requirements, where growth in conventional fuels continues
alongside lower-carbon alternatives. Refining expansion, petrochemical integration, natural gas and clean energy businesses therefore
progressed in parallel rather than in sequence.

The approach combined energy security with investments in emerging energy value chains. Green hydrogen, renewable power and
Sustainable Aviation Fuel featured prominently in this effort, while petrochemical integration assumed greater importance within
refinery expansion projects and long-term asset planning.

The successful implementation of SPRINT in its first year established a disciplined framework for translating strategic priorities
into measurable business outcomes. Building on this strong foundation, the programme has now been expanded to encompass
additional strategic priorities, including Exploration & Production, cost optimisation across logistics, refining, marketing, and
pipeline operations, new business development, Research & Development, and other critical business functions.

As SPRINT continues to evolve, it will serve as a common execution framework for delivering IndianOil’s long-term strategic
priorities across the enterprise. By aligning business objectives with clearly defined initiatives, measurable milestones, and robust
accountability mechanisms, the programme will strengthen execution discipline, enhance operational performance, accelerate
technology adoption, advance the energy transition, and create sustained value for all stakeholders.

Risk Management                                                                                                                                MD&A




Managing Risk, Sustaining Growth
Energy markets have entered a period where shocks travel faster and last longer
than in previous commodity cycles. A disruption in shipping routes quickly
becomes a freight issue, then a refining margin issue, then a working capital issue
and eventually a consumer demand issue. The distinction between geopolitical,
financial and operational risks is therefore becoming increasingly blurred.
For India, the implications are amplified by import dependence across crude oil, LNG and several petrochemical feedstocks. For
IndianOil, the challenge lies not in the availability of demand, but in preserving affordability, availability and profitability through periods
of disruption, volatility and structural change. IndianOil addresses these exposures through a combination of sourcing diversification,
refining flexibility, infrastructure scale and capital discipline. The wider crude slate reduces concentration risk and provides greater
flexibility in procurement decisions under evolving market conditions.

Business Highlights of Major Group Companies

Value Across the Group
 CHENNAI PETROLEUM CORPORATION LTD. (CPCL)
 Subsidiary (51.89% Holding)


 CPCL became a subsidiary of IndianOil in 2001. Its integrated refinery at Manali, Tamil Nadu, produces transportation fuels,
 lubricants, waxes and petrochemical feedstocks, serving the energy requirements of southern India and IndianOil’s refining
 and petrochemical value chain.

     Operational Highlights
     y Commissioned its first retail outlet in Tamil Nadu under the ‘Sooper’ brand.

     y Conferred ‘Navratna’ status in 2026 by the Government of India.

     y Received the ICAI Gold Shield for Excellence in Financial Reporting and maintained its governance record for 21
       consecutive years.

     y Recorded its highest-ever crude throughput of over 11.7 MMT, with revenue of ₹78,611 Crore and consolidated Profit
       After Tax of ₹3,103 Crore in 2025–26.




 Future Aspiration
 CPCL plans to pursue refinery modernisation, energy efficiency and digitalisation, alongside measures aimed at raising operating
 performance across its business. These initiatives are expected to add to IndianOil’s refining and petrochemical presence in
 southern India.




 IOC GLOBAL CAPITAL MANAGEMENT IFSC LTD. (IGCMIL)
 Wholly Owned Subsidiary (100% Holding)


 IndianOil became the first corporate in India to establish a Global/Regional Corporate Treasury Centre (GRCTC) in GIFT
 City through the incorporation of IGCMIL in 2023. The Company serves as the treasury centre for IndianOil and its group
 companies across geographies. It also acts as an investment holding platform for managing overseas investments and
 facilitating global investments.


     Operational Highlights
     y Cumulative financial transactions crossed USD 1 billion across India, the US, Singapore, UAE, Sri Lanka and Mauritius
       by 2025-26.

     y Earned USD 20 million in interest income and USD 1.93 million in operating profit during the year.

     y Facilitated a USD 78.3 million equity investment in Sun Mobility Pte Ltd., Singapore.




 Future Aspiration
 IGCMIL aims to become the central treasury hub for the IndianOil Group, providing treasury, financing, investment and risk
 management solutions while tapping opportunities available through GIFT City.

LANKA IOC PLC
Subsidiary (75.12% Holding)


Incorporated in 2002, Lanka IOC PLC (LIOC) undertakes petroleum marketing operations in Sri Lanka. Over two decades, it
has emerged as the country’s second-largest oil marketing company, with businesses spanning retail fuels, lubricants, LPG,
aviation fuel, bunkering and petrochemicals.


 Operational Highlights
 y Operates an integrated downstream business through a network of retail outlets and fuel infrastructure across Sri Lanka.

 y Ranked 6th among Sri Lanka’s Top 100 listed companies by revenue.

 y Received awards for Integrated Reporting, Financial Reporting and Corporate Governance during the year.

 y Its ‘Propel’ lubricant brand was recognised as ‘Supplier of the Year’ by the Plastics & Rubber Institute of Sri Lanka.

 y Reported consolidated revenue of ₹8,155 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹355 Crore during the year.


Future Aspiration
LIOC plans to expand its bunkering infrastructure and add new offerings across lubricants and petrochemicals. It also plans to
pursue partnerships for entry into renewable energy.




IOCL SINGAPORE PTE. LTD. (ISPL)
Wholly Owned Subsidiary (100% Holding)


Incorporated in 2016, ISPL manages IndianOil’s investments in international oil and gas exploration and production assets and
is intended to establish trading of fuel and related products. Its portfolio includes producing assets in Russia and Oman and
exploration assets in Abu Dhabi, providing access to international hydrocarbon resources.



 Operational Highlights
 y A hydrocarbon discovery was announced in Abu Dhabi’s Onshore Block-1 during 2025-26, where IndianOil is one of the joint
   operators through an SPV.

 y Recorded consolidated revenue of ₹2,403 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹1,732 Crore in 2025-26.




Future Aspiration
ISPL aims to maximise production from existing assets, progress the Abu Dhabi discovery towards commercialisation and pursue
opportunities to increase reserves and production across its overseas oil and gas portfolio.

 INDIANOIL (MAURITIUS) LTD. (IOML)
 Wholly Owned Subsidiary (100% Holding)


 Incorporated in 2001, IOML established IndianOil’s downstream presence in Mauritius. Its business spans retail fuels,
 aviation fuel, bunkering, lubricants and industrial fuels, while also serving as a platform for exploring opportunities across
 the African region.


     Operational Highlights
     y Operates a network of retail outlets and has a presence across key petroleum product segments in Mauritius.

     y Holds 51% market share in aviation turbine fuel.

     y Ranked among the Top 10 Companies in Mauritius in 2025.

     y Serves as IndianOil’s gateway for exploring business opportunities across the African region.

     y Reported consolidated revenue of ₹2,589 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹92 Crore during the year.


 Future Aspiration
 IOML plans to grow its core petroleum marketing business, add supply chain and storage infrastructure, advance digitalisation
 and diversify into energy-related services. It will also pursue business opportunities across the African continent.




 PETRONET LNG LTD. (PLL)
 Associate (12.50% Holding)


 Incorporated in 1998 as an associate of IndianOil, ONGC, GAIL and BPCL, PLL develops and operate LNG import and
 regasification infrastructure in India. Its operations contribute to reliable LNG imports and India’s natural gas supply.



     Operational Highlights
     y Maintained operational reliability, safety and efficiency while providing uninterrupted regasification services.

     y Serves natural gas demand across industrial, power, City Gas Distribution and other sectors.

     y Reported consolidated revenue of ₹43,495 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹3,913 Crore during the year.




 Future Aspiration
 PLL plans to expand regasification capacity, pursue opportunities across the LNG value chain and develop international partnerships
 to serve India’s natural gas requirements and long-term energy security.

HINDUSTAN URVARAK & RASAYAN LTD. (HURL)
Joint Venture (29.67% Holding)


Incorporated in 2016 as a joint venture of IndianOil, NTPC, Coal India, FCIL and HFCL, HURL operates three ammonia-urea
complexes at Gorakhpur, Sindri and Barauni. With combined urea production capacity of around 3.8 MMTPA, its operations
contribute to India’s fertiliser self-sufficiency and food security.


 Operational Highlights
 y Operated all three plants at approximately 100% capacity utilisation during the year.

 y Recorded its highest-ever operational and financial performance, backed by higher production and sales.

 y Achieved urea sales exceeding 5.3 MMT in 2025-26.

 y Reported consolidated revenue of ₹21,217 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹2,457 Crore.

 y Received awards across logistics and supply chain management, digitalisation, corporate communications and corporate
   social responsibility.


Future Aspiration
HURL plans to invest in research and development and explore organic and inorganic growth opportunities to contribute to India’s
long-term fertiliser security.




INDIAN SYNTHETIC RUBBER PVT. LTD. (ISRPL)
Joint Venture (50% Holding)


Incorporated in 2010 as a 50:50 joint venture between IndianOil and TSRC Corporation, Taiwan, ISRPL operates India’s first
world-scale E-SBR facility at Panipat, Haryana. The Company manufactures Emulsion Styrene Butadiene Rubber (E-SBR) for
domestic tyre manufacturers, reducing dependence on imports.


 Operational Highlights
 y Operated its 120 KTPA E-SBR manufacturing facility at Panipat and recorded its highest-ever sales of 128 KT during the year.

 y Initiated plans to expand manufacturing capacity and diversify into Solution Styrene Butadiene Rubber (S-SBR) for next-
   generation and electric vehicle tyres.

 y Received the Apollo Tyres Gold Partner Award and the CEAT Outstanding Performance in Quality Award.

 y Reported revenue of ₹2,026 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹315 Crore in 2025-26.




Future Aspiration
ISRPL plans to expand production capacity and diversify into advanced specialty rubber products to serve changing requirements
across the automotive and electric mobility sectors.

 INDIANOIL ADANI VENTURES LTD. (IAVL)
 Joint Venture (50% Holding)


 Established in 1996, IAVL, formerly Indian Oiltanking Ltd., is a joint venture between IndianOil and Adani Ports & Special
 Economic Zone Limited. The Company develops, owns, operates and maintains bulk liquid storage terminals and refinery tank
 farm infrastructure, alongside Operations & Maintenance (O&M) services.


     Operational Highlights
     y Progressed two major refinery tank farm projects at Paradip and Panipat, scheduled for commissioning during 2026-27.

     y Received the GSS National Safety Award and World Safety Organisation India OHS&E Awards for occupational health and
       safety.

     y Reported consolidated revenue of ₹507 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹294 Crore during the year.




 Future Aspiration
 IAVL plans to expand its geographical presence, grow its Operations & Maintenance services and develop energy logistics
 infrastructure.




 INDIANOIL PETRONAS PVT. LTD. (IPPL)
 Joint Venture (50% Holding)


 Incorporated in 1998, IPPL is a joint venture between IndianOil and Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS), Malaysia.
 The Company develops, owns and operates LPG import terminals, storage facilities and associated logistics infrastructure for
 the import, storage, terminalling and distribution of LPG.


     Operational Highlights
     y Operated LPG import terminals at Haldia (1.2 MMTPA) and Ennore (0.6 MMTPA), supported by associated bottling plants
       and logistics infrastructure.

     y Handled nearly 3.9 MMT of LPG during the year.

     y Diversified into MS and HSD, with three remote retail outlets in Arunachal Pradesh.

     y Received several safety recognitions, including the Golden Peacock Occupational Health & Safety Award 2025 for the Haldia
       Terminal, CII Safety Awards, NSCI Awards and World Safety Organisation India OHS&E Awards.

     y Reported consolidated revenue of ₹3,135 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹266 Crore during the year.



 Future Aspiration
 IPPL seeks to deliver sustainable growth while maintaining high standards of safety, governance and environmental stewardship.

INDIANOIL SKYTANKING PVT. LTD. (IOSPL)

Incorporated in 2006, IOSPL provides aviation fuel infrastructure services across fuel farm management, into-plane fuelling
and Operations & Maintenance (O&M). The Company pioneered the Open Access Model for fuel farm operations and
introduced Single Man Refuelling in India.


 Operational Highlights
 y Operates fuel farm facilities at Bengaluru & NOIDA Airport, provides into-plane fuelling services at Delhi, NOIDA and
   Mumbai airports, alongside O&M services at multiple AFS locations.

 y Handled over 3.2 MMT of aviation fuel during 2025-26.

 y Received the Wings India 2026 – Best Fuel Service Provider Award for the fourth time.

 y During 2025-26, IndianOil Skytanking Pvt. Ltd. reported a Consolidated Revenue of ₹306 Crore and Profit After Tax of
   ₹51 Crore.



Future Aspiration
IOSPL plans to broaden its capabilities in aviation fuel infrastructure development and technical consultancy. The Noida International
Airport is expected to add to its business growth.




INDIANOIL LNG PVT. LTD. (IOLPL)
Joint Venture (45% Holding)


Established in 2015, IOLPL owns and operates the 5 MMTPA LNG import, storage and regasification terminal at Kamarajar
Port, Ennore, Tamil Nadu. The terminal forms part of IndianOil’s natural gas infrastructure and serves LNG demand in southern
India.


 Operational Highlights
 y Provides LNG unloading, storage and regasification services for IndianOil following the commencement of commercial
   operations in 2019.

 y Reported revenue of ₹482 Crore and Profit After Tax of ₹220 Crore.




Future Aspiration
IOLPL plans to provide reliable and uninterrupted regasification services to IndianOil, pursue business opportunities through
strategic collaborations and raise utilisation of its LNG infrastructure as India’s natural gas market grows.

To mitigate crude oil supply risks and elevated oil prices, the Company diversified its crude procurement portfolio by increasing imports
from other geographies and optimised refinery operations to process the alternative crude grades, while maintaining planned refinery
throughput and operational continuity. Further, your Company demonstrated exceptional agility in ensuring uninterrupted natural gas
supplies by proactively sourcing spot LNG cargoes from diversified geographies, including the USA, Angola, Indonesia, Trinidad &
Tobago, Nigeria and Oman. Despite logistical challenges arising from disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, the Company maintained
supply continuity to critical sectors such as fertilizers and City Gas Distribution (CGD). There has also been a renewed momentum
towards accelerating the development of Piped Natural Gas (PNG) infrastructure to enhance long-term energy security by supporting
the transition towards cleaner and more reliable energy.

Through these timely and decisive interventions, your Company successfully balanced household energy security, industrial requirements
and supply-chain resilience, reinforcing its role as a dependable energy partner to the nation during the period of geopolitical uncertainty.

Annexure – II
ANNUAL REPORT ON CSR ACTIVITIES FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-26

1.   A brief outline of the Company's CSR policy
     IndianOil’s Sustainability & Corporate Social Responsibility (S&CSR) Policy is guided by a vision to deliver energy solutions in a
     manner that is efficient, safe, and ethical, while optimising environmental impact and enhancing the quality of life of communities.
     The Policy underscores Company’s commitment to achieving sustainable growth for both the business and the nation. In alignment
     with this vision, IndianOil’s mission focuses on creating shared value for stakeholders and growing in harmony with society. It
     emphasises the optimal utilisation of resources, integration of environmental and social considerations into business decisions.
     The Policy also reinforces IndianOil’s commitment to building trust and goodwill as a responsible corporate citizen through
     transparency, ethical conduct, and responsible business practices. Additionally, it promotes the adoption of technological and social
     innovations to drive sustainability and contribute meaningfully towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Support for Higher Secondary School, Bongaigaon,

BGR Higher Secondary School (BGRHSS), Bongaigaon, established
in 1984, stands as a key educational institution serving the local
community. The institution was upgraded to a higher secondary                             Enriching lives at Child Development Centre, Lok Nayak Hospital, New Delhi

results in board examinations. BGRHSS currently caters to around

Right to Education (RTE) Act, providing access to quality education

Swarn Jayanti Samudayik Hospital, Mathura
Swarn Jayanti Samudayik Hospital (SJSH), Mathura, Uttar Pradesh,
reflects IndianOil’s sustained commitment to strengthening
community healthcare services. Operational since 1999, the
hospital is a 50-bed facility, with dedicated provisions for patients
from Below Poverty Line (BPL) families and caters to the medical
needs of residents in Mathura and nearby areas. The hospital offers
accessible and affordable healthcare through free and subsidised
consultation and treatment services. Equipped with essential
medical infrastructure viz., modern operation theatre, advanced
diagnostic laboratory, intensive care unit (ICU), and specialised
departments, SJSH ensures comprehensive care across a range
of medical needs. In addition, this hospital actively extends its
outreach through health camps and awareness programmes in
the surrounding rural areas, promoting preventive healthcare and
early diagnosis. On an average, about 51,000 patients benefit from
the hospital each year. During 2025–26, IndianOil contributed H6.13               Beneficiary of IndianOil Arogyam (Mobile Medical Unit) of Mathura Refinery
Crore towards operation and maintenance of this hospital.
                                                                                Assam Oil College of Nursing (AOCN), Digboi
                                                                                Assam Oil College of Nursing (AOCN), Digboi, Assam, established
                                                                                in 1986, reflects IndianOil’s commitment to strengthening
                                                                                healthcare capacity in the North-Eastern region. AOCN offers a
                                                                                three-year Diploma in General Nursing & Midwifery (GNM) and a
                                                                                four-year B.Sc. (Nursing) programme, aimed at building a skilled
                                                                                nursing workforce. With an annual intake of 30 students in each
                                                                                course, the programs focuses on equipping young women with
                                                                                the professional competencies required for quality patient care.

                                                                                Over the years, AOCN has developed into a credible institution for
                                                                                nursing education, with its B.Sc. (Nursing) programme introduced
                                                                                in 2014 to further expand opportunities for advanced training.
                                                                                Since inception, the college has produced 610 GNM graduates
                                                                                and 231 B.Sc. (Nursing) graduates, maintaining an excellent track
                                                                                record of 100% placement. During 2025–26, IndianOil contributed
 Glimpse of Swarn Jayanti Samudayik Hospital (SJSH), Mathura
                                                                                H3.88 Crore towards operation and support for the college.


Assam Oil Division (AOD) Hospital, Digboi
Assam Oil Division (AOD) Hospital at Digboi, Assam, stands as
a longstanding pillar of healthcare in the North-Eastern region,
with its origins dating back to 1939. Over the years, the 200-bed
facility has evolved into a well-equipped multi-specialty tertiary
care hospital, catering to the medical needs of people residing in
remote and underserved areas. The hospital offers a wide range
of specialties viz., Medicine, Surgery, Orthopaedics, Obstetrics &
Gynaecology, Paediatrics, Ophthalmology, ENT, Pathology, and
Radiology etc. The hospital houses the first dedicated Burn Unit
in North-East India, supported by modern equipment and trained
medical personnel. In addition to its clinical services, the hospital
plays a proactive role in community healthcare by organising
health camps and outreach programmes in nearby rural areas,
thereby improving awareness and access to essential medical
services. The facility continues to serve as a critical healthcare
provider in the region, treating over 8,200 (non-entitled) patients
annually on an average. During 2025–26, IndianOil contributed
H5.67 Crore towards operation & maintenance of this hospital.

(B) Efforts made towards Technology Absorption, Adaptation and Innovation:
    As a continuous effort towards improvement of product pattern, product quality, improvement of energy efficiency as well as
    to meet the dynamic environmental emission norms and to improve profit margin, your Company has adopted most modern
    technologies in line with the latest worldwide developments in the field of petroleum refining and petrochemicals production.

    Major technologies adopted by the Company are as under: -

    i)     Indigenous Technology (adopted during 2025-26) & benefits derived :
                IndEcoP2F® Technology
			             INDEcoP2F® Technology at Digboi Refinery converts waste plastics, including PE, PP, and multi-layer packaging, into
                valuable fuels within the Delayed Coker Unit (DCU) refinery. This technology offers over 95% conversion efficiency
                with low capital expenditure and can be implemented without refinery shutdown or throughput reduction. The entire
                development, including basic and detailed engineering of the improved INDEcoP2F Demo Unit, was completed in-
                house by the R&D team of the Company, reflecting the true spirit of ‘Make in India’ and showcasing the commitment to
                sustainable and cost-effective solutions. Continuous mode operation of the INDEcoP2F demo unit commenced in 170
                kTA DCU of Digboi Refinery in September 2025.

                Bio-VR technology
			             Addressing CPCB’s mandate of 90% Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) reduction from refinery ETPs, the Company
                has developed and successfully commissioned the Bio-VR technology at Barauni Refinery. The conventional carbon
                bed-based VOC removal systems face rapid saturation, high replacement and regeneration costs, and risks related to
                hazardous spent carbon disposal and secondary emissions. This proprietary Bio-VR technology offers a sustainable,
                cost-effective alternative to conventional carbon-based systems and strengthens IndianOil’s commitment to
                environmental compliance.

    ii)    Details of imported technology (imported during the last three years reckoned from the beginning of the financial year)
		         No technology was imported during the last three years.

(b) Nomination and Remuneration Committee
    The Company being a Government Company, the appointment, including the terms and conditions of appointment of the Directors
    are decided by the Government of India. However, the Board has constituted a Nomination and Remuneration Committee to:

    -    approve certain perquisites for Whole-time Directors and below Board level executives as well as to approve performance-
         related pay to the executives of the Company as per the DPE guidelines;

    -    create and sanction posts as well as to consider and approve promotions to Grade ‘I’ i.e., Senior Management Personnel.

    The performance evaluation of the Directors (including Independent Directors) has not been carried out by the Nomination &
    Remuneration Committee, as the Company being a Government Company, the powers relating to evaluation of Directors vests
    with the Government of India. Such evaluation is exempted for Government Companies under the provisions of the Act.

    As mentioned hereinabove, the Nomination and Remuneration Committee was discontinued w.e.f. March 28, 2026 due to non-
    availability of Independent Directors on the Board.

(c) Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee
­­   The Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee has been constituted in line with the provisions of Regulation 20 of SEBI (LODR) and
     Section 178 of the Act. The terms of reference of the committee inter-alia include:

     -       Resolving the grievances of the security holders of the listed entity including complaints related to transfer/transmission of
             shares, non-receipt of annual report, non-receipt of declared dividends, issue of new/duplicate certificates, general meetings etc.

     -       Review of measures taken for effective exercise of voting rights by shareholders.

     -       Review of adherence to the service standards adopted by the listed entity in respect of various services being rendered by the
             Registrar & Share Transfer Agent.

     -       Review of the various measures and initiatives taken by the listed entity for reducing the quantum of unclaimed dividends and
             ensuring timely receipt of dividend warrants/annual reports/statutory notices by the shareholders of the company.

     The Committee also approves issuance of share certificates/letter of confirmations. The Company endeavours to resolve
     complaints / grievances / queries of stakeholders / investors within a reasonable period of time.

     As mentioned hereinabove, the Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee was discontinued w.e.f. March 28, 2026 due to non-
     availability of Independent Directors on the Board.

(d) Corporate Social Responsibility & Sustainable Development Committee (CSR & SD)
    The CSR&SD committee has been constituted in line with the provisions of Section 135 of the Act. The terms of reference of the
    committee inter-alia include:

    a)   Formulate and recommend to the Board, a Corporate Social Responsibility Policy which shall indicate the activities to be
         undertaken by the Company as specified in Schedule VII in areas or subject, specified in Schedule VII.

    b)   To operate its activities in providing energy solutions to its customers in a manner that is efficient, safe & ethical, which
         optimises the impact on environment and enhances quality of life of the community, while ensuring sustainable growth of
         business and the nation.

    c)   Recommend the amount of expenditure to be incurred on the activities referred to in clause (a).

    d)   Monitor the Corporate Social Responsibility Policy of the Company from time to time.

    e)   Institute a transparent monitoring mechanism for implementation of the CSR projects or activities.

    As mentioned hereinabove, the CSR&SD Committee was discontinued w.e.f. March 28, 2026 due to non-availability of Independent
    Directors on the Board.

     The quarterly unaudited financial results and annual audited financial results are announced within the time prescribed under the
     SEBI (LODR). The results are published in leading newspapers like The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Hindu Business

     members over e-mail. The Company issues news releases on significant corporate decisions / activities and host them on its
     website as well as informs the stock exchanges as and when deemed necessary.

Management Discussion and Analysis
1.   Industry Structure and Developments
1.1 ECONOMIC PERFORMANCE AND OUTLOOK
     The global economy remained resilient during 2025 despite operating in an environment of heightened geopolitical uncertainty, rising
     trade fragmentation, and persistent financial vulnerabilities. Global GDP growth remained steady at around 3.4% in 2025, unchanged
     from 2024, supported by resilient domestic demand in several major economies, technology-led investments, and accommodative
     financial conditions, including a weaker US Dollar.

     Advanced economies recorded modest growth of around 1.9% in 2025, marginally higher than 1.8% in 2024, while growth in Emerging
     Market and Developing Economies (EMDEs) eased slightly to 4.4% from 4.5%. Among major economies, the United States grew by
     2.1%, moderating from 2.8% in 2024 due to tighter financial conditions and slower consumption, although labour markets remained
     resilient. The Euro Area’s growth improved to 1.4% from 0.9%, supported by easing inflation and stronger domestic demand. China’s
     growth remained at 5.0%, despite continued weakness in the property sector, subdued consumer confidence, and rising trade‑related
     disruptions from tariffs and shifting global supply chains.

     India continued to remain the fastest-growing major economy in the world, with GDP growth rising to 7.7% in 2025-26 from 7.1% in
     the previous year. Growth was supported by strong domestic consumption, sustained public infrastructure investments, resilient
     services activity, improving manufacturing momentum, and continued policy support.

3.4. ENABLERS: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION, COST OPTIMISATION AND INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITY
     In an increasingly volatile global energy environment marked by geopolitical uncertainty, supply chain disruptions, rapid
     technological change, and evolving consumer expectations, IndianOil continues to strengthen the institutional capabilities required
     to remain agile, competitive, and future-ready. Your Company’s long-term strategy is focused on building a digitally enabled,
     operationally efficient, innovation-driven, and resilient enterprise capable of sustaining growth while supporting India’s evolving
     energy transition journey.

3.4.1. Digitalisation, AI and Technology Integration
     IndianOil is increasing the use of digital platforms, advanced analytics, artificial intelligence and automation across refining,
     pipelines, marketing, supply chain and customer-facing operations. Ongoing investments in enterprise systems, digital customer
     ecosystems, operational intelligence platforms and AI-enabled applications are improving planning, monitoring and decision-
     making across businesses. At the same time, technology deployment is supporting greater operational visibility, process efficiency,
     asset utilisation and customer responsiveness, while reducing manual intervention across several business processes.

Independent Auditors’ Report
To
The Members of IndianOil Corporation Limited


Report on the Audit of the Standalone Financial Statements
Opinion
We have audited the accompanying standalone financial statements of IndianOil Corporation Limited (the “Company”), which
comprise the Balance Sheet as at March 31, 2026, the Statement of Profit and Loss (including Other Comprehensive Income), the
Statement of Changes in Equity and the Statement of Cash Flows for the year ended on that date and notes to the financial statements,
including a summary of material accounting policies and other explanatory information (hereinafter referred to as the “Standalone
Financial Statements”).

In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, the aforesaid Standalone Financial
Statements give the information required by the Companies Act, 2013 (the “Act”) in the manner so required and give a true and fair view
in conformity with Indian Accounting Standards specified under section 133 of the Act read with the Companies (Indian Accounting
Standards) Rules 2015, as amended and other accounting principles generally accepted in India, of the state of affairs of the Company as
at March 31, 2026, and profit including other comprehensive income, changes in equity and its cash flows for the year ended on that date.

Basis for Opinion
We conducted our audit of the Standalone Financial Statements in accordance with the Standards on Auditing (SAs) specified under
section 143(10) of the Act. Our responsibilities under those Standards are further described in the Auditors’ Responsibilities for the
Audit of the Standalone Financial Statements section of our report. We are independent of the Company in accordance with the Code of
Ethics issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (“ICAI”), together with the ethical requirements that are relevant to our
audit of the Standalone Financial Statements under the provisions of the Act and the Rules thereunder, and we have fulfilled our other
ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements and the ICAI’s Code of Ethics. We believe that the audit evidence we have
obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion on the standalone financial statements.

Emphasis of Matter
We draw attention to Note 9 of the Standalone Financial Statements in respect of LPG and Crude Oil shipments waiting at the Arab
Gulf / Persian Gulf region as on March 31, 2026. Attention is also invited to Note 49.7 regarding the geopolitical developments in the
Middle East region.

Our opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.


Key Audit Matters
Key audit matters are those matters that, in our professional judgment, were of most significance in our audit of the Standalone Financial
Statements of the current period. These matters were addressed in the context of our audit of the Standalone Financial Statements as a
whole, and in forming our opinion thereon, and we do not provide a separate opinion on these matters. We have determined the matters
described below to be the key audit matters to be communicated in our report:

Information Other than the Standalone Financial Statements and Auditors’ Report Thereon
The Company’s Board of Directors is responsible for the preparation of the other information. The other information comprises the
information included in the Management Discussion and Analysis, Board’s Report including Annexures to Board’s Report, Business
Responsibility and Sustainability Report, Corporate Governance, but does not include the Standalone Financial Statements and our
auditors’ reports thereon.

The above referred information is expected to be made available to us after the date of this audit report.

Our opinion on the Standalone Financial Statements does not cover the other information and we do not express any form of assurance
conclusion thereon.

In connection with our audit of the Standalone Financial Statements, our responsibility is to read the other information identified above
when it becomes available and, in doing so, consider whether the other information is materially inconsistent with the Standalone
Financial Statements, or our knowledge obtained in the audit or otherwise appears to be materially misstated.

When we read other information, if we conclude that there is a material misstatement therein, we are required to communicate the
matter to those charged with governance and take appropriate actions necessitated by the circumstance and the applicable laws and
regulations. We have nothing to report in this regard.


Responsibilities of Management and Those Charged with Governance for the Standalone Financial Statements
The Company’s Board of Directors is responsible for the matters stated in section 134(5) of the Act with respect to the preparation of
these Standalone Financial Statements that give a true and fair view of the financial position, financial performance, total comprehensive
income, changes in equity and cash flows of the Company in accordance with the accounting principles generally accepted in India,
including the Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) specified under section 133 of the Act. This responsibility also includes maintenance
of adequate accounting records in accordance with the provisions of the Act for safeguarding of the assets of the Company and for
preventing and detecting frauds and other irregularities; selection and application of appropriate accounting policies; making judgments
and estimates that are reasonable and prudent; and design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal financial controls,

In preparing the Standalone Financial Statements, the Board of Directors is responsible for assessing the Company’s ability to continue
as a going concern, disclosing, as applicable, matters related to going concern and using the going concern basis of accounting unless
the management either intends to liquidate the Company or to cease operations, or has no realistic alternative but to do so.

The Board of Directors is also responsible for overseeing the Company’s financial reporting process.


Auditors’ Responsibilities for the Audit of the Standalone Financial Statements
Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the Standalone Financial Statements as a whole are free from material
misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditors’ report that includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high
level of assurance but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with SAs will always detect a material misstatement
when it exists. Misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, they could
reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of these Standalone Financial Statements.

As part of an audit in accordance with SAs, we exercise professional judgment and maintain professional scepticism throughout the
audit. We also:

      Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the Standalone Financial Statements, whether due to fraud or error, design
      and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks, and obtain audit evidence that is sufficient and appropriate to provide a
      basis for our opinion. The risk of not detecting a material misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from
      error, as fraud may involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control.

      Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the
      circumstances. Under section 143(3)(i) of the Act, we are also responsible for expressing our opinion on whether the Company has
      adequate internal financial controls with reference to Standalone Financial Statements in place and the operating effectiveness of
      such controls.

      Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of accounting estimates and related disclosures
      made by management.

      Conclude on the appropriateness of management’s use of the going concern basis of accounting and, based on the audit evidence
      obtained, whether a material uncertainty exists related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the ability of the
      Company to continue as a going concern. If we conclude that a material uncertainty exists, we are required to draw attention in our
      auditors’ report to the related disclosures in the Standalone Financial Statements or, if such disclosures are inadequate, to modify
      our opinion. Our conclusions are based on the audit evidence obtained up to the date of our auditors’ report. However, future events
      or conditions may cause the Company to cease to continue as a going concern.

      Evaluate the overall presentation, structure and content of the Standalone Financial Statements, including the disclosures,
      and whether the Standalone Financial Statements represent the underlying transactions and events in a manner that achieves
      fair presentation.

We communicate with those charged with governance regarding, among other matters, the planned scope and timing of the audit and
significant audit findings, including any significant deficiencies in internal control that we identify during our audit.

We also provide those charged with governance with a statement that we have complied with relevant ethical requirements regarding
independence, and to communicate with them all relationships and other matters that may reasonably be thought to bear on our
independence, and where applicable, related safeguards.

From the matters communicated with those charged with governance, we determine those matters that were of most significance in the
audit of the Standalone Financial Statements of the current period and are therefore the key audit matters. We describe these matters in
our auditors’ report unless law or regulation precludes public disclosure about the matter or when, in extremely rare circumstances, we
determine that a matter should not be communicated in our report because the adverse consequences of doing so would reasonably
be expected to outweigh the public interest benefits of such communication.

Annexure B to the Independent Auditors’ Report
(Referred to in Paragraph 2 under “Other legal and regulatory requirements “of our report of even date)

Annexure referred to in Independent Auditors’ Report to the members of IndianOil Corporation Limited on the
standalone financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2026

1.    Assess the fair valuation of all the investments, both quoted and unquoted, made directly by the Company
      or through Trusts, for Post retirement benefits of the employees. This includes verifying valuation
      methodologies, ensuring consistency with Ind AS and reviewing supporting documentation. The auditor
      shall provide a brief note on the valuation approach, its reasonability, and compliance with applicable
      regulations, reporting any material deviations or misstatements.
      Our Reply:
      We have assessed the fair valuation of investments, both quoted and unquoted, made through Trusts established for post-
      retirement employee benefits (no such investments being directly made by the Company). Fixed income securities such as GOI
      Securities, SDLs and corporate bonds have been valued using discounted cash flow methodology based on applicable market
      yield curves and duration-based yields. Mutual Funds and ETFs have been valued based on NAV declared by AMFI, whereas
      Investment Trusts have been valued based on the last traded market price as on the valuation date. Deposits and LIC policies have
      been considered at their carrying/book value as a reasonable approximation of fair value. Based on our examination, the valuation
      methodologies applied are generally consistent with the requirements of the applicable accounting framework and are considered
      reasonable. No material deviations or misstatements were observed in respect of the valuation of the aforesaid investments
      during the course of our audit.


2.    Whether the Company has a system in place to process all accounting transactions through an IT system? If
      yes, whether review of this system and controls significant to the Company’s financial reporting process as
      well as cyber security has been done by Information Security Auditing Organisations empanelled by Cert-
      In at a minimum frequency of once in a year and material discrepancies found, if any, have been suitably
      reported. The implications of processing accounting transactions outside the IT system on the integrity of
      accounts along with the financial implications may also be reported.
      Our Reply:
      The Company has an established system whereby all accounting transactions are recorded in the SAP ERP system either directly
      or through SAP-integrated IT systems. However, certain computations such as closing stock valuation, provision for taxation,
      expected credit loss assessment and similar year-end accounting estimates are carried out outside the SAP environment due to
      the complexity of such computations, involvement of significant external inputs and the need for extensive validation and review
      prior to accounting. These computations are primarily performed during the process of closing of books of accounts. We observed
      that the complete financial impact of such computations is thereafter recorded in SAP through a defined maker-checker control
      mechanism and that the financial statements are generated from the SAP system. Further, no material accounting transactions
      processed outside the IT system, which could have an adverse impact on the integrity of accounts or financial statements,
      were observed.

      Based on the information and explanations provided by the Management, the review of IT systems, application controls, general IT
      controls and cyber security framework significant to the Company’s financial reporting process has been carried out by Information
      Security Auditing Organisations empanelled with CERT-In at the prescribed periodicity of at least once in a year. The reports issued
      by such agencies and the corrective actions taken by the Management on the observations, wherever applicable, have also been
      reviewed. However, no material discrepancies were reported.

3.   Whether funds (grants/ subsidy etc.) received/ receivable for specific schemes from Central/State
     Government or its agencies were properly accounted for as per the applicable accounting standards or
     norms and whether the received funds were utilised as per its terms and conditions? Whether accounting
     of interest earned on grants received has been done as per terms and conditions of the Grant. List the cases
     of deviation.
     Our Reply:
     Based on the audit procedures performed by us and according to the information and explanations provided by the Management,
     the Company has properly accounted for funds (grants / subsidy etc.) received/ receivable for specific schemes from Central/
     State Government or its agencies, as the case may be, as per the applicable accounting standards or norms. The received funds
     were utilised as per its terms and conditions. Further, accounting of interest earned on grants received has been done as per terms
     and conditions of the grant.


4.   Whether the Company has identified the key Risk areas? If yes, whether the Company has formulated any
     Risk Management Policy to mitigate these risks? If yes,
     (a)   whether the Risk Management Policy has been formulated considering global best practices?
		Our Reply:
		         Based on the audit procedures performed by us and according to the information and explanations provided by the
           Management, the Company has identified key risk areas relevant to its operations and also formulated a Risk Management
           Policy approved by the Board.

		         As informed by management, the policy has not been specifically benchmarked against any global framework, however based
           on our review of the policy framework, related documents and discussions with the Management, the Risk Management
           Policy appears to have been formulated broadly considering globally accepted risk management principles and practices.
           The policy also provides for periodic monitoring and review of identified risks and mitigation measures.

     (b)   whether the Company has identified its data assets and whether it has been valued appropriately?
		Our Reply:
		         Based on the audit procedures performed by us and according to the information and explanations provided by the Management,
           the Company has not separately identified or recognised any data assets requiring valuation in the financial statements.


5.   Whether the Company is complying with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) (Listing
     Obligation and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and other applicable rules and regulations of
     SEBI, Department of Investment and Public Asset Management, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Department
     of Public Enterprises, Reserve Bank of India, Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, CERT-IN, Ministry of
     Electronics and Information Technology and National Payments Corporation of India wherever applicable?
     If not, the cases of deviation may be highlighted.
     Our Reply:
     Based on the audit procedures performed by us and according to the information and explanations provided by the Management,
     in respect of the year under audit, the Company is generally complying with the applicable provisions of the Securities and
     Exchange Board of India (SEBI) (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and other applicable rules
     and regulations issued by regulatory authorities including Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM),
     Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Department of Public Enterprises, Reserve Bank of India, Telecom Regulatory Authority of India,
     CERT-In, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and National Payments Corporation of India, wherever applicable
     to the Company.
